summary:
In long-duration space missions, radiation, isolation, altered gravity and closed environments affect astronauts’ health and create bone, immune, cardiovascular and behavioral risks. When contact with Earth is no longer immediate, the crew must assess their own health without being experts.
SelfCheck is a real-time health monitoring system with two role-based views: a quick view for the crew member and a control center for health professionals, with charts of each variable’s evolution. It processes 57 variables across seven body systems and the habitat using medical rules backed by NASA and WHO sources, applies thresholds adjusted to in-flight evidence from NASA’s Human Research Program, warns about clinical combinations, and explains what each indicator measures and what to do if a value goes out of range.
Its impact is reflected in two areas:
1. Medical: it gives the crew autonomy, links values into clinical alerts and distinguishes adaptation from risk.
2. IT: it provides a real-time event architecture with rules kept outside the code, traceable and reproducible, plus reusable open source (Apache 2.0). It is a demonstration with simulated data; its thresholds must be validated by flight surgeons.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

SelfCheck is a real-time health monitoring system for a four-person crew on long-duration space missions. It receives each crew member's measurements as they happen (57 variables across seven body groups: radiological, cardiovascular and respiratory, hematological and immunological, musculoskeletal and bone, metabolic/renal/nutritional, neurological/cognitive/behavioral, and digestive/general symptoms) plus a shared habitat group (CO2, noise, dust). A rules engine classifies every value into one of four states: Normal, Observation, Alert or Not evaluable. It also explains what each indicator measures and what to do when it goes out of range.

It has three screens:

- Quick view, for the crew member: a live ECG that beats at their real heart rate, an overall status and one card per body system. From here they can report that they are training or request medical assistance.

- Control center, for the medical team on board: the whole crew, vital signs, a chart of every variable over the mission, the medical history and an alert log with clinical combinations, such as a high heart rate with low blood pressure.

- Simulator, which runs the demo: it speeds up the mission clock and triggers scenarios such as atrial fibrillation, fever from infection, dehydration, sustained poor sleep, a solar particle event or a CO2 scrubber failure.

BENEFITS

Far from Earth, communication is delayed and a doctor is not always available. SelfCheck lets the crew understand their health at a glance and act early. It gives the medical team on board the detail and the history they need. Every threshold is backed by NASA sources: NASA-STD-3001, Human Research Program in-flight evidence, OCHMO technical briefs and JSC-67378 nutrition requirements.

INTENDED IMPACT

To support crew autonomy on long missions by lowering the cognitive load of reading dozens of measurements a day, catching problems sooner and making each recommendation clear. SelfCheck is open source (Apache 2.0) so others can build on it.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Backend: Kotlin 2.2 on Java 21 and Spring Boot. Apache Kafka with Kafka Streams runs the rules engine, with Avro schemas and Schema Registry for the messages. TimescaleDB (PostgreSQL) with Flyway stores the history.

- Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite and Apache ECharts, served with nginx.

- Medical rules: a YAML knowledge base with a source for each threshold.

- Build and run: Gradle and Docker Compose. 122 automated tests.

- No special hardware: everything runs in a browser, and the demo is live at https://selfcheck.earth.

CREATIVITY

- The ECG is animated at the crew member's real heart rate and changes shape wiation, for example, is drawn as irregular beats without P waves.

- Clinical combinations link several variables into a single alert.

- Daily calorie and fluid targets are computed for each crew member with NASA f

- Thresholds use in-flight evidence where NASA publishes it, instead of Earth reference ranges.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Missing or expired data is never shown as healthy: it is Not evaluable.

- Some rules need several days in a row before raising a state, which avoids false alarms.

- Context matters: heart rate is only evaluated at rest and glucose only when f

- Some cuts depend on sex.

- One situation raises one alert.

- The habitat has its own state and does not change any crew member's status.

- States are shown with color, icon and label.

- The interface is in English and Spanish, with day and night themes.

- All crew data is simulated and anonymous. SelfCheck is a demonstration, not a
